units.t: Memory & Learning. Episode two.
In this episode: How to learn anything faster, Focus and deep work and Mindset: can you get smarter.
Part one. How to learn anything faster.
Most study habits people use feel effective but aren't.
Here are the techniques learning scientists actually recommend.
Methods that underperform.
In 2013, psychologist John Dunlosky and colleagues reviewed hundreds of studies on ten common learning techniques.
Highlighting, rereading and summarising, the favourites of most students, were rated low.
They create a feeling of familiarity: the page looks known, so we mistake recognition for being able to recall and use the material.
Our sense of how well we're learning is unreliable.
A 2019 Harvard study found physics students taught with active, problem-based methods learned more, yet felt they had learned less than students given polished lectures.
Psychologists call this the illusion of competence.
Judge learning by testing yourself, not by how comfortable a session felt.
If studying feels a little like hard work, that's often a good sign.
Testing and spacing.
The two best-rated techniques cost nothing and take no more time.
First, retrieval practice: close the book and write down everything you remember, then check what you missed.
Use flashcards, but say the answer before flipping.
Answer practice questions or explain the topic aloud as if teaching a friend.
Pulling information from memory strengthens it and shows what you don't know yet.
Check your answers promptly.
Second, spacing: return to material across several sessions, perhaps a day later, then a few days, then a week or two.
In the 1970s, Sebastian Leitner popularised a flashcard box system: cards move to a box reviewed less often when you get them right, and back to the first when you miss.
Modern apps automate this.
Mix it and connect it.

Most textbooks group practice: twenty problems of type A, then twenty of type B. Interleaving mixes them: A, C, B, A, C. It feels messier and scores during practice are usually worse, but later performance is better, because you learn to recognise which approach each problem needs.
It works best for related skills that are easy to confuse, like different equations or tennis shots.
Elaborative interrogation means asking why and how: why does this happen, and what would change if it were different?
Connect new information to your own life or to concrete examples.
Learning about inflation?
Think about what bread cost when you were a child.
Pairing words with diagrams helps too.
The more hooks a fact has, the easier it is to find again.
The Feynman technique.
Physicist Richard Feynman, a Nobel laureate, was famous for explaining complex ideas in plain, lively language.

The technique named after him has four steps: pick a concept, explain it in simple words as if to a 12-year-old, notice where you stumble or reach for jargon, then return to the source to fill those gaps and simplify again.
If you can't explain it simply, you probably don't fully understand it yet.
It combines retrieval practice with elaboration, and it's a quick, honest check on whether you've really learned something or just recognise the words.
The basics that matter.
No technique beats the basics.
Sleep consolidates memories, and all-nighters before exams harm recall.
Short, focused sessions with breaks beat long, distracted ones, so put the phone away.
Regular exercise supports brain health and mood.
Curiosity helps: when you're curious about a question, you remember not only the answer but other things around it.
Finally, the popular 'learning styles' idea, that people learn best only visually or aurally, isn't supported by evidence; a 2008 review found no good studies backing it.
Match the method to the material instead.
The key idea: Rereading, highlighting and summarising feel useful but produce weak learning, because familiarity isn't knowledge.
Part two. Focus and deep work.
Your attention is your most valuable resource, and your phone is designed to take it.
How to get it back.
Designed to distract.
Social media, news and many games make money from your attention, so they're designed to keep you scrolling.
Infinite feeds, notifications and autoplay use behavioural psychology.
Unpredictable rewards are especially compelling: like a poker machine, you never know whether the next refresh will bring something good.
Former tech designers, such as Tristan Harris, have spoken publicly about how this is engineered.
Distraction is partly a design problem, not just a personal weakness.
Switching costs you too.
Researcher Sophie Leroy described 'attention residue': part of your mind stays on the previous task, hurting performance on the new one, especially if the first was unfinished.
Some studies link even a silenced phone on your desk to slightly lower performance, though results are mixed.
Close your open loops.
Incomplete tasks keep popping into mind, pulling attention from what you're doing now.
In 2011, psychologists E.
J. Masicampo and Roy Baumeister found that reminding people of an unfinished goal made their minds wander more and hurt performance on an unrelated task.
But when people wrote down a specific plan for when, where and how they would finish it, the interference largely disappeared, even though the task was still undone.
Cal Newport builds on this with an end-of-day 'shutdown ritual': review what's unfinished, note the next step for each, then genuinely stop thinking about work.
Deep work and flow.
Cal Newport coined 'deep work' in his 2016 book for distraction-free concentration that pushes your abilities to their limit: writing, coding, analysis, learning hard skills.
'Shallow work' is logistical, easily interrupted tasks like email.
Newport argues deep work is becoming rarer just as it becomes more valuable.
Most people manage only a few hours of it a day, so protect those hours.
Psychologist Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi studied moments when people become so absorbed that time vanishes, and called it flow.
It tends to arise with clear goals, immediate feedback and a challenge slightly beyond your skill.
Too easy bores; too hard causes anxiety.
A single notification can break flow.
Your attention's rhythm.
In World War II, the RAF wanted to know why radar operators hunting submarines missed more signals as their watch wore on.
Psychologist Norman Mackworth's 'clock test' found accuracy fell within the first half-hour.
This vigilance decrement has since been found in lifeguards, security screeners and drivers, which is why screening jobs rotate staff and road-safety campaigns urge breaks at least every two hours.
Alertness also varies by time of day.
For most people it climbs through the morning, dips after lunch and partly recovers later, though night owls peak later.
A 2016 Danish study of around two million test results found children scored lower later in the day, and a 20 to 30 minute break beforehand more than made up for an hour's decline.
Guard your sharpest hours for hard thinking.
Rest is part of focus.
Attention gets tired.
Real breaks, like walking, stretching or looking out a window, restore it better than switching to your phone, which keeps the brain busy with new information.
Some research suggests that time in nature, even a short walk through a park, helps restore attention.
Letting yourself be bored occasionally, without reaching for a screen, gives the mind space to wander, which is linked to creativity and problem-solving.
And sleep is non-negotiable: sleep deprivation seriously impairs concentration, memory and judgement.
Focus isn't about grinding longer; it's about alternating real effort with real rest.
The key idea: Many apps are designed to capture your attention, and switching tasks leaves 'attention residue'.
Part three. Mindset: can you get smarter.
Believing you can improve does matter, but the famous research is more modest than the posters suggest.
Fixed versus growth.
Stanford psychologist Carol Dweck proposed that people hold different beliefs about ability.
With a fixed mindset, you believe talent is set at birth, so failure means you're not smart.
With a growth mindset, you believe abilities develop through effort, good strategies and help from others, so failure is information.
Most people hold a mix, varying by area.
Her 2006 book Mindset became hugely popular in schools and workplaces.
In a 1998 study with Claudia Mueller, children were praised either for being smart or for working hard.
Those praised for intelligence chose easier tasks, enjoyed the work less, did worse after a setback, and some overstated their scores.
Those praised for effort chose harder tasks and persisted.
Praise process, not fixed traits.
The brain does change.
Neuroscience supports the idea that abilities can grow.
In a 2004 study, adults who spent three months learning to juggle showed increased grey matter in brain areas that process visual motion, and the gains partly faded once they stopped.
Similar changes appear in musicians and language learners.
Intelligence test scores are fairly stable in adults, and genes play a real role, but skills and expertise can be built substantially.
Anders Ericsson found experts use deliberate practice: working on specific weaknesses, just beyond your comfort zone, with clear goals and quick feedback.
Playing a song you know is not the same as drilling the bar you keep fumbling.
The popular '10,000-hour rule' oversimplified his work; talent, starting age and opportunity also matter.
The replication debate.
As mindset went global, researchers tested it at scale.

A large 2019 study of over 12,000 US high school students found a short online growth-mindset lesson had a small positive effect on grades, mainly for lower-achieving students, and mostly in schools whose culture supported the message.
Some meta-analyses found overall effects near zero, while others argued well-designed programs help specific groups.
The honest summary: mindset matters somewhat, but it's not a magic fix, and simply putting up posters or telling people to 'have a growth mindset' does little on its own.
False growth mindset.
Dweck herself warned about a 'false growth mindset': praising effort even when it's not working, or claiming a growth mindset without changing behaviour.
Trying hard with the wrong approach leads to frustration and, eventually, the fixed belief that you can't do it.
Effort is the fuel, but strategy is the steering.
'You worked hard' is less useful than 'That approach didn't work; what could you try next?'
How adults react to failure may matter more than what they say.
A 2016 study by Kyla Haimovitz and Dweck suggested parents' beliefs about intelligence didn't pass directly to children; their reactions to failure mattered more: disaster, or chance to learn.
Teams that review mistakes without blame tend to learn faster.
Using it wisely.
Practical takeaways that fit the evidence: notice when you think 'I'm just not a maths person' and replace it with 'I'm not good at this yet'.
See mistakes as feedback, and ask what specifically went wrong.
Compare yourself to your past self, not to others.
Choose challenges slightly beyond your level, and look for good teachers, coaches or resources rather than relying on effort alone.
And be kind to yourself: believing you can improve isn't the same as expecting to be instantly good, and progress in anything real, from guitar to a new job, takes time.
The key idea: Carol Dweck's research suggests children praised for effort, not intelligence, take on harder challenges.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Why do rereading and highlighting feel effective but work poorly?
Answer. They feel familiar, which we mistake for knowing.
Question two. What is 'attention residue'?
Answer. Your mind lingering on the previous task.
Question three. What happened to children praised for being smart rather than for effort?
Answer. They avoided challenges and wilted after setbacks.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
